newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH FEB CPI EASES AS CENTRAL BANK POLICIES BITE.
newsitem.headline: CZECH FEB CPI EASES AS CENTRAL BANK POLICIES BITE.

text.p: Czech consumer inflation eased in February, with analysts predicting a further slowdown in coming months as the central bank's tight monetary policy continues to bite.

The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) said on Monday that month-on-month CPI eased to 0.3 percent from 1.2 percent in January, a typically high inflation month, putting the year-on- year figure at 7.3 percent, down from 7.4 percent the previous month.
The key sliding average inflation figure, which uses 1993 as a base, edged down to 8.6 percent from 8.7 percent in January, and was down from 9.1 percent in February 1996.

"The figure is encouraging, though we expect that inflation will slow throughout the first half of the year because of the central bank's monetary tightening moves last year," said Boris Gomez, a macro-economic analyst at ING Barings.

Last summer the Czech National Bank (CNB) raised its key discount rate one percentage point to 10.5 percent, and hiked minimum reserve requirements to 11.5 percent from 8.5 percent to squeeze off surging domestic demand.

The moves have appeared to significantly slow growth in the money supply, which at 9.7 percent in November was well below the central bank's 13 to 17 percent growth target for 1996, and in the middle of its 8-12 percent range for 1997.
But central bank officials have warned that wage growth -- which was up 14.4 percent in nominal terms in January -- and its influence on inflation is a growing concern.
"Question marks may come to the forefront in the second half when we will have a better idea of wage growth and some price deregulations," Gomez added.
CSU figures show price deregulation influenced the seasonally-adjusted rate by 0.63 percent, while seasonally-adjusted core inflation by 0.34 percent.
Analysts added that they were pleasantly surprised with CSU figures showing that prices of foodstuffs, drinks and tobacco, which usually push inflation up, were unchanged month-on-month.
Despite the gradual downtrend over the past few months, most analysts agreed that there seems little chance the CNB would ease its tight monetary policy in the near future.
Curbing inflation has been at the heart of almost all of the CNB's policies, and both CNB and government officials have said they expect rates to remain high, at least over the near-term.

"The figures appear to prove the positive results of the CNB's monetary policy. If the rate downtrend continues, it may allow for the rational consideration of a lowering of rates," said Miroslav Soucek, an analyst at bank IPB.
